articles.title_orig: Salesforce deepens AI bets with $5.66 billion Braze deal
articles.title_zh: Salesforce deepens AI bets with $5.66 billion Braze deal
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Salesforce slipped roughly 1% on Tuesday morning, after the company announced an agreement to buy customer engagement platform Braze for about $5.66 billion.
Under the deal, holders of Braze Class A common stock will get $47.50 in cash per share, with the transaction expected to close in fiscal 2028, according to a Salesforce blog .
Braze shares closed at $30.04 on Monday. The stock skyrocketed more than 50% on Tuesday after a brief halt premarket following the news. The company makes artificial intelligence marketing tools to manage customer data and messaging.
"Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we'll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us," Bill Magnuson, CEO of Braze, said in a statement. "Salesforce's platform will help us innovate faster and together we'll help marketers around the world build deeper, more lasting relationships with their customers."

articles.title_orig: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.title_zh: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.content_orig:
Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.
The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options.
"We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own."
The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.
While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.
The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices.
In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street.
Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.
Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period.
The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%.
Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits.
The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

articles.title_orig: Wall St opens lower as AI stocks decline, oil prices rise
articles.title_zh: Wall St opens lower as AI stocks decline, oil prices rise
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices surged in early trading Tuesday, as energy markets adjusted to a new normal in the Middle East. The increase in crude prices threatened to drive up the cost of gas in the United States just two weeks ahead of the midterm elections.
U.S. crude prices jumped as much as 5% to about $109 a barrel, the highest price since April, while the price of international Brent crude climbed 1.5% to more than $111, its highest price since May. Prices pulled back later in the morning, after weaker than expected U.S. housing starts raised the prospect of a broader slowdown and lower demand.
Prices for advanced oil contracts dated for next year also hit record highs, “ implying an extended period of high oil prices deep into 2027,” analysts with Deutsche Bank said in a note published Tuesday.
“The 2027 contracts are moving higher as well as the possible reality of higher for longer oil prices sink in,” said Peter Boockvar, author of the Boock report and Chief Investment Officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners, said in a note published Tuesday.
High gas prices have become a major issue for voters in the midterms, where Republicans’ face dwindling odds of maintaining their control of Congress.
A recent NBC News poll found that 67% of U.S. adults believe gas prices are a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. A majority also said that current economic conditions have caused them to change their spending habits.
U.S. gasoline prices had started off the week lower. At $4.28 a gallon, the national average price of unleaded was on pace to reach its lowest level in a month.
But that trend is likely to be upended as higher crude prices filter through to the pump.
Several factors were contributing to Tuesday’s oil price hikes.
The cost of chartering a large tanker vessel to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz has quadrupled since September, data show.
Much of that increase is a risk premium, both for sailors and insurance. During the past two weeks, at least 18 ⁠vessels have been attacked in the strait, the ship-tracking group Kpler said in a note ⁠Monday.
The higher cost of transport has begun to offset the recent bump in supply from a growing number of ships moving through the strait.
The Iranian attacks on ships have also prompted investor speculation that the Trump administration will be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms, the Deutsche Bank analysts said.
Iran-aligned Houthi rebels also claimed Monday they had hit airport, energy and military targets in Saudi Arabia, as well as a ​training camp in Yemen for that government’s security forces.
The U.K. will begin deploying fighter jets over Saudi Arabia to help protect against further Houthi attacks, the defense ministry said Tuesday.
The entry of another country’s military into the regional hostilities was taken as a further sign of escalating tensions.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: EU unveils Arctic strategy to counter increasing Russia, China influence
articles.title_zh: EU unveils Arctic strategy to counter increasing Russia, China influence
articles.content_orig:
The European bloc is stepping up some of its efforts in the resource-rich region, but says it still wants fossil fuels to stay in the ground
The European Commission has presented an updated strategy for the Arctic as climate change and rapidly melting ice open up the remote but resource-rich region.
“With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition,” said European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday.
With the new strategy, the commission aims for the EU to keep pace with rivals as new shipping routes and mining opportunities, including for critical raw materials, become available.
“Access to Arctic sea lanes and natural resources is of strategic interest to the EU,” Kallas said.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambles to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war . Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”
Witkoff will be meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb will also join the talks, it added.
Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.
Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.
In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.
Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.
When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”
Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.
Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“ The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
articles.title_zh: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
articles.content_orig:
Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says
The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek , as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.
A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.
The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment.
“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.
Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned.
Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.
DeepSeek has been contacted for comment.
One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.
The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.
The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.
Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.
The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

articles.title_orig: China’s hybrid car exports to EU surge by more than 200% as import cap looms
articles.title_zh: China’s hybrid car exports to EU surge by more than 200% as import cap looms
articles.content_orig:
Exports climbed to nearly 100,000 vehicles in September ahead of limits due to take effect at the end of the year
China’s hybrid car exports to the European Union tripled in September from a year earlier, with shipments expected to remain elevated before an import cap agreed during recent trade talks takes effect.
The country shipped nearly 100,000 hybrid cars to the bloc last month, up 18.9 per cent from August and 204.2 per cent from a year earlier, customs data showed on Tuesday.
The surge outpaced a 142.7 per cent year-on-year rise in China’s total exports of passenger cars to the EU. Analysts said the rapid growth likely reflected carmakers front-loading vehicles ahead of high-level negotiations held in Beijing in early October.
“Dealerships may have sought to get as many purchases in as possible before potential quotas or tariffs ahead of trade talks,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING.

articles.title_orig: France Protests Show Europe’s Shift Away From Centrist Politics
articles.title_zh: France Protests Show Europe’s Shift Away From Centrist Politics
articles.content_orig:
Interior minister confirms military to reinforce police as Italy poised to approve tougher security measures in response to protests
And back to the debate in the French parliament, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, confirmed that military forces will be deployed to reinforce police during the upcoming protests on Saturday.
“We will ⁠deploy the Sentinelle force, ​obviously ‌as a substitute ‌to interior security ‌forces... mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order,” Nuñez ‌told the National Assembly.
He added that the response to any unrest will be “firm.”
As reported earlier, PM Lecornu said the police presence on the weekend would be “massive,” as the government wants to see an immediate return to order after last weekend’s riots ( 15:29 ).
Elsewhere, there are some positive news from Romania, where Luca Niculescu has been confirmed as the country’s new prime minister in centrist president Nicușor Dan’s fourth attempt at getting a new government in place.
Niculescu, a former journalist and diplomat who served as Romania’s ambassador to France , is expected to form a government led by ministers from the centre-left Social Democratic party and some technocrats – although it remains a very open question how long he will last in the post.
Back to France , the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told lawmakers of plans for “massive” deployment of police forces ahead of further protests expected on Saturday.
In a passionate speech in the parliament, Lecornu framed the situation as a choice “between violence the Republic,” as he doubled down on his claims that the protests morphed into “an insurrectionary scheme led by far-left and ultra-left groups.”
He insisted that “a return to order is the prerequisite for everything else,” stressing he also wants to address the substantive requests posed by the student movement.
He also acknowledged some issues with the police planning and intelligence gathering so far.
Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto has warned that recent riots in Milan and other parts of Italy were part of a broader “hybrid war” against the West, the Italian news agency Ansa reported.
Speaking at a conference in Rome, Crosetto said:
“ The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras; they are the product of what I call hybrid warfare – a form of conflict being waged against our nations through unconventional tools like TikTok, social media, and YouTube … The West has yet to realise this or take any meaningful action in response.”
“If three out of every 10 young people took part in these demonstrations – and I am not just referring to ‘maranza’ (youth gangs) or second-generation Italians – and if six out of 10 agree with these sentiments, it is because they have been subjected to a ‘counter-education’ from somewhere – not from their families or schools.
This has instilled in them values, ambitions, a worldview, and points of reference that stand in direct conflict with the society we live in and with our democratic rules.”
As we mentioned in a previous post , US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy which are aimed at ending the war with Russia.
It comes as relations between Zelenskyy and the US president, Donald Trump, are at their lowest since their public fallout in the Oval Office last year .
Only yesterday, Zelenskyy said the US was deliberately delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, deepening the public spat with Trump. He has also said that Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening.
As the diplomacy in Oslo takes place to end the war, we are seeing more reports of deadly Russian attacks on Ukraine. Four people were killed and 27 others injured, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, according to regional police.
Three people were killed and six were injured in the Obukhiv district , where warehouses were damaged, police said. This morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway , Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.
Meanwhile, Portuguese police cleared protest camps in ⁠Lisbon and Porto before ⁠dawn, removing activists who had occupied two central squares to protest against a worsening housing crisis, and making 55 arrests, Reuters reported.
Activists ⁠had occupied Lisbon’s Rossio square since Saturday, pitching around 200 tents, and Porto’s Dom Joao I square for around 10 days.
The ⁠camps mirrored housing protests in neighbouring Spain, and coincided with unrest over rising ​living costs in countries such as ‌ France , Belgium and Italy.
Italy is poised to approve new security measures after parts of the country were rocked by waves of protests over the weekend.
Italy’s deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini , said that as part of the crackdown police will be able to detain under-18s at police stations for 12 hours, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger.
“We want to intervene quickly on young people,” Salvini told the RTL ​radio broadcaster ahead of a cabinet meeting to approve the measures, which have not yet been formally announced.
The security crackdown will also reportedly include banning gatherings for people deemed a threat to public order.
Thousands of people peacefully protested against living costs in cities across northern Italy over the weekend, but a number of the marches turned violent with some demonstrators seen looting stores and clashing with police.
Several hundred protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze ‌and looted shops in the centres of Milan, where more than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend.
In southern Italy, farmers and truckers have been blockading ports and highways to protest against the surge in fuel prices resulting from the US-Israel war on Iran.
France will offer interest-free loans of up to €50,000 to businesses affected by the riots and looting over the weekend, economy minister Roland Lescure said.
The scheme is expected to open on Friday, and should help traders with cash flow issues as they seek to get insurance payouts, the minister said, quoted by French media.
First court cases are also being progressed, with justice minister Gérald Darmanin confirming that 149 people have been put in provisional detention or imprisoned as part of ongoing trials. In a separate TV appearance on Monday evening, he said around 2,500 remained in custody for questioning, Reuters reported.
The number is expected to go up, as BFMTV reported that some 40 people are expected to appear in front of Parisian courts this afternoon.
In other news, it looks like France may have another problem coming its way, with heavy rainfall in the south of the country.
Parts of Corsica are now under a red alert for rain and flooding, with local flooding observed last night in several towns and village in the region. An all-time rainfall record broken in Salon-de-Provence, BFMTV reported.
The Gard department is on orange alert, with the coastal areas on a yellow alert.
Some flooding was also reported near Marseille .
As well as Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy will also meet the Norwegian prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre and the Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s new King Haakon during his visit to Oslo.
Jared Kushner is scheduled to attend digitally.
Ahead of the talks, Støre said that Zelenskyy has asked Norway and Finland to arrange a meeting as part of the ongoing diplomatic work, at a critical time for Ukraine. “Together with president Stubb, I am pleased to have such a meeting here in Oslo.”
Afterwards there will be a press conference with Zelenskyy, Stubb and Støre and Zelenskyy has been invited for an audience at the palace.

articles.title_orig: Data center stocks slide as Korea IPO plunges 30%, pressuring tech sentiment
articles.title_zh: Data center stocks slide as Korea IPO plunges 30%, pressuring tech sentiment
articles.content_orig:
Data center stocks struggled Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave.
Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity.
The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities. CoreWeave shares lost 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 4%. Iren was down about 6%.
HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away.
"Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds ," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside.
Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters . Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses.
Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out.
Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates.
Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note.
Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030.
"Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said.
Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC.
"At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."
Chip stocks are also feeling some pain on Tuesday. Micron is down close to 2% as of market open; AMD is down about 1.5%; and Nvidia is down about 1%.

articles.title_orig: GM beats on Q3 results, tightens profit outlook, and unveils new $20 billion buyback
articles.title_zh: GM beats on Q3 results, tightens profit outlook, and unveils new $20 billion buyback
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
GM ( GM ) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates, tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.
For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 versus $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.
But the big update was guidance. For the full year, GM now expects:
Adjusted EBIT of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion (prior $14 billion to $16 billion)
Adjusted EPS of $12.75 to $13.75 (prior $12 to $14)
Adjusted automotive free cash flow of $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion (prior $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion)
Investors were hoping for more, as the stock is getting hit in early trading, down over 5%.
Both ranges keep the same midpoints as before — $15 billion and $13.25 billion — meaning GM trimmed the upside as much as the downside.
GM also lifted its adjusted automotive free cash flow forecast to $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion from $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.
GM's board approved a new $20 billion multiyear authorization with no expiration date. GM also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.18 per share.
"We think this is a proven strategy," GM CEO Mary Barra wrote in her letter to shareholders. "The new $20 billion multiyear share repurchase authorization we announced today further demonstrates our board's commitment to creating even greater shareholder value."
Barra also said GM is working to continue its momentum "despite growing inflationary pressures."
This is seen with GM's costs creeping up. GM now expects commodity inflation of about $2 billion (the top of its prior $1.5 billion-$2 billion range), including logistics and memory chip (DRAM) costs. It also cut its expected regulatory benefits to about $500 million from as much as $750 million. Offsetting that, gross tariff costs are tracking toward the low end of its $2.5 billion-$3.5 billion range.
Earlier this month, GM reported third quarter US sales of 670,974 vehicles , a drop of 5.5% compared to a year ago, as a collapse in EV sales offset gains from its pickups and small SUVs .
Based on GM's model-by-model figures, EV sales fell about 62% to roughly 25.5K units, shrinking to under 4% of GM's US volume from more than 9% a year ago. Excluding EVs, GM's sales were essentially flat, up 0.3%.
Sales of the Chevrolet Equinox EV plunged 92.4% to 1,905, the Blazer EV dropped 84.4%, the GMC Hummer EV slid 72.9%, and the Cadillac Lyriq fell 50.5%.
GM's gas-powered trucks helped deflect EV losses. Light-duty pickup sales rose 9.3%, led by a 13.3% jump in the Chevrolet Silverado light-duty to 100,221, while the GMC Sierra light-duty gained 2.9%. Heavy-duty models were softer, with the Silverado HD down 10.1% and the Sierra HD off 6.9%. GM said it is on track to lead the full-size pickup segment for a seventh straight year.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu outlines his vision for the future of Iran’s Islamic regime on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’
A new coalition of Iranian opposition groups in the restive southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman in the Islamic Republic have launched a string of armed attacks against the clerical regime in the region.
The six strikes claimed by the coalition known as the People’s Fighters Front (JMM) have contributed to instability in the provinces, raising pressing questions about whether armed resistance against the clerical regime in Tehran will spread and if the regime can retain control over Sistan and Baluchistan, which is a majority Iranian Sunni province.
Iran is largely a Shiite Muslim country, and the minority Iranian Sunni population has faced discrimination over the decades. Sistan and Baluchistan is the second largest of the 31 Iranian provinces.
MOJTABA KHAMENEI DEFIES ‘MALICIOUS’ ATTACKS AS US ARMY ZEROES IN ON IRAN’S 350,000 TROOPS
Sistan and Baluchistan, Iran. (Mohammad /Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital, "The Sunni unrest can stretch the regime's military and internal security capabilities and have a psychological impact on its forces, in addition to what they experienced during the 40-day operation by the U.S. and Israel . The armed groups would not be able to establish control of the south-east, but they can seriously weaken the regime's control."
He added, "Whether these forces are receiving assistance from the Islamic Republic's adversaries — being that the Gulf Arab states or even Israel and the U.S. — remains an open question."
Protesters and members of Iranian paramilitary Basij forces march next to the fourth generation Khorramshahr ballistic missile Khaibar displayed during an anti-Israeli rally to show their solidarity with Palestinians in Tehran on Nov. 24, 2023. (Photo by Hossein Beris/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
According to an October Human Rights Activist News Agency (HRANA) report , "The pace of violence accelerated significantly in recent weeks [in the provinces] with 18 incidents recorded in just the final 18 days of the reporting period, surpassing the total for any previous full month."
JMM coalesced as an opposition coalition in Dec. 2025 through an amalgam of Baloch nationalist organizations with the militant Sunni group Jaish al-Adl.
HRANA documented "at least 63 armed incidents were recorded across Iran’s southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman between March 31 and Oct.10, 2026, amid a sharp escalation in armed violence in the region."
The armed resistance resulted in "at least 94 people dead and 33 injured, while official sources reported 87 fatalities and 10 injuries."
IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS
A woman member of the Basij paramilitary, affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guard, holds a machine gun on a pickup truck during a parade of pro-government Iranian women. (Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)
The Baloch coalition stunned the regime on Oct. 14 with the assassinations of women members of the Basij paramilitaries, including a commander and a police officer in Sistan and Baluchistan Province. The Basij has been designated a terrorist entity by the U.S. government because it falls under the American-classified terrorist movement Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Just days before the attack on the female Basij commander, Iranian regime-controlled media reported that Nosrat Eftekhari, deputy for Cultural and Social Affairs of the Provincial Law Enforcement Command, was killed by a roadside bomb in Zahedan, Sistan and Baluchistan provinces.
Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "There have been periodic cycles of unrest in Sistan and Baluchistan Province over the years. What we are now witnessing is an uptick in such activity. The current commander of the IRGC’s Ground Forces, Mohammad Karami used to be governor of the province and commanded IRGC forces there. His experience in the province was one of the reasons Karami was elevated to the post in 2025 given the sensitive security situation in the country."
Brodsky continued that "I don’t see any imminent threat in terms of such a seizure of control, but a red line for Iranians, especially in the opposition, is preserving the territorial integrity of Iran. That needs to be understood in Western capitals."
MOTORCYCLE PATROLS SWARM IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the ground forces, navy, air force and air defense force. (Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Khalilullah Balochi, who is a Baluch activist and journalist, told Iran International that "The activities of these groups are not new; what is new is the intensification of attacks."
JMM’s devastating attacks targeting the brutal Iranian regime have generated attention from Iranian dissidents and experts.
Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital "The newly formed popular Fighters Front has carried out a series of relatively successful attacks against mid-level regime officials and security personnel in Sistan and Baluchistan province in recent months, drawing a degree of public attention. At a time when the regime is executing protesters on a daily basis, the killing of certain mid-ranking security and military operatives has been met with some satisfaction among segments of Iranian society."
He warned, however, that "Nevertheless, the Iranian public remains deeply cautious and largely distrustful of such groups. Two major concerns underpin this distrust: the possibility of separatist ambitions and the influence of radical Islamism, which is fundamentally at odds with the increasingly secular outlook of Iranian society."
AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS
Iranians gather while blocking a street during a protest in Tehran, Iran on Jan. 9, 2026. (MAHSA/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
Mohebbi sees encouraging signs from the JMM, including "the coalition’s recent statements, unlike the rhetoric traditionally associated with similar groups, contain no explicit references to Baluch separatism. Instead, the coalition has identified its primary objective as dismantling the system of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist) and liberating the country from its oppression. It has explicitly declared that it seeks ‘an Iran for all Iranians."’
He continued that "The reality is that these groups lack the capacity to confront the regime in conventional warfare . Through guerrilla operations, however, they can inflict significant psychological blows on the regime and its security establishment. Whether their activities can gain traction beyond Sistan and Baluchistan will depend largely on their ability to sustain what appears to be an effort to earn broader public trust."
Beni Sabti, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Israel, told Fox News Digital the coalition has "a lot of guns" and created an "armed rebellion" against the Iranian regime in the provinces. He said, however, the armed upheaval is limited to the region Baluchistan.
Sabti, who was born in Tehran, said the clerical regime in the capital Tehran does not exercise solid control over the provinces, which resembles parts of South America where some governments lost sovereignty to militias.

articles.title_orig: Is CoreWeave the Silicon Valley Bank of 2026?
articles.title_zh: Is CoreWeave the Silicon Valley Bank of 2026?
articles.content_orig:
AI stocks rallied on Monday, but CoreWeave closed slightly lower as investors remained skittish about its debt. Yields on Oracle debt also remained elevated as credit worries persist across the AI trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite gained 1% on Monday. Oracle rose 1% after dropping 9% last week, while Intel climbed 2.4%, Advanced Micro Devices added 1.8 % and Micron Technology rose 3%.
CoreWeave , the so-called neocloud company that led the sell-off last week, bounced around, hit a 52-week low and ultimately closed fractionally lower. Meanwhile, its bond yields remained high and its five-year credit default swaps were at distressed levels.
The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 was at 14.9%, slightly down from its high of over 15% last week. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps stood at roughly 1,082 basis points, nearly 2% lower than Friday.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. A spread above 1,000 basis points is generally a sign of distress.
"The market tends to get worried about companies that have refinance risk when rates are higher, and CoreWeave was a little bit of the poster child," said John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson. His firm's multi-sector income fund owns CoreWeave 2031 bonds. "They need the debt markets in order to grow, in some form or fashion."
The concern wasn't limited to CoreWeave's bonds. It was also seen in Oracle, which is an investment-grade hyperscaler and considered a bellwether on AI credit. Its five-year CDS spread also moved wider on Monday to 315 basis points, a 311% increase from a year prior.
What's notable is the dispersion in AI-related high-yield bonds, similar to what is happening in the broader junk market, Goldman Sachs said last week.
Neoclouds and firms with significant frontier lab exposure are largely at the epicenter of the funding cost debate, while AI-adjacent energy and utilities have been more resilient since they have more diversified revenue streams and a relatively defensive earnings profile, Amanda Lynam, Goldman's chief credit strategist, said in a note. Investment-grade bonds have also seen  less severe price action, she added.
"As the pace of issuance has increased, differentiation factors around construction risk, coverage of principal or refinancing risk, and claim to tenant have become increasingly important," Lynam wrote. "Additional considerations around power availability, permitting, and insurance all advocate for a bottom-up approach to investing in the asset class."
Economist David Rosenberg, founder and president of Rosenberg Research, called Oracle the "canary in the coal mine." Oracle, Alphabet , Amazon and Meta have issued more than $228 billion of bonds this year and now account for about 10% of the global investment-grade market, he noted.
Oracle, which has about $132 billion of net debt and a BBB- rating from S&P Credit Ratings, "is the bridge between junk-rated neoclouds and investment-grade hyperscalers,"  said Rosenberg, who has a reputation for bearish calls.
"A downgrade to junk would be the clearest sign of contagion."

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?
articles.content_orig:
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.
Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.
The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.
For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.
In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.
This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.
He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.
Yet the photographs tell a different story.
Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.
While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.
There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.
China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened.
South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.
The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.
In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.
So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.
North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.
Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.
Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader.
Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.
Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.
But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.
All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.
The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.
Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.
If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.
Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.
Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.
Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.
The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.
So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it.
He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.
Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

articles.title_orig: China slams US ban on DeepSeek AI over security concerns
articles.title_zh: China slams US ban on DeepSeek AI over security concerns
articles.content_orig:
China fired back at the Trump administration Tuesday after the U.S. government ordered federal civilian agencies to remove Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek's products from their systems, citing national security concerns and the risk that Beijing could gain access to sensitive American data.
The Department of Homeland Security ordered agencies to remove DeepSeek products and services, including third-party technology developed using its AI models, and prohibited future purchases, according to a notice made public Monday in the Federal Register.
The order, issued in July, warned that DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," citing concerns that the company's China-based servers could potentially expose sensitive U.S. data to Chinese authorities.
Beijing criticized the ban, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning accusing Washington of politicizing technology.
"China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues," Mao told reporters Tuesday.
Mao added that Beijing would "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies."
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.
The dispute comes ahead of a planned November meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, where AI is expected to be on the agenda.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
China launched a new state-owned data enterprise Tuesday aimed at strengthening its position in the global artificial intelligence race as Beijing moves to expand the development and use of data resources critical to advancing AI technology.
The National Data Group, headquartered in Xiongan, roughly 60 miles southwest of Beijing, will serve as a national platform to promote data sharing across industries and regions, according to state media.
The group will also work with various stakeholders to develop China's data economy, explore new business models and expand the market, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang attended Tuesday's inauguration ceremony, saying the group's establishment was important for capitalizing on opportunities in artificial intelligence and strengthening China's competitive edge, according to state media.
The announcement comes amid intensifying technological competition between Washington and Beijing, including a recent U.S. ban on Chinese AI startup DeepSeek's products across federal civilian agencies over national security concerns.
China established its National Data Administration in 2023 to oversee data policy, while the new National Data Group will focus on market operations and putting data resources to use.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Boeing unveiled a new artificial intelligence-powered platform Tuesday designed to help airlines anticipate aircraft maintenance needs, identify emerging risks and make faster operational decisions using data collected across their fleets.
The platform, called Dataliner, was developed in partnership with Microsoft and uses AI to combine aircraft maintenance records, operational information and Boeing's engineering expertise to give airlines a more complete picture of their fleets.
Built using Microsoft's Azure AI Foundry and other technologies, Dataliner aims to help airlines move beyond analyzing individual aircraft to identifying maintenance trends and potential problems across entire fleets.
"Airlines have more data available to them than ever before, but turning that data into meaningful action remains a challenge," said Lindsey Douglas, vice president of Cabin, Modifications, Maintenance and Digital Services at Boeing Global Services.
Douglas said the platform will help customers "anticipate maintenance needs, identify emerging risks and take timely action."
Boeing said airlines will retain control over their data, including what information they share, while the platform uses encryption, access controls and monitoring to protect sensitive aviation information.
Dataliner will also support the development of new Boeing digital services, including an AI-powered tool for airline technical operations and aircraft lifecycle planning.
Artificial intelligence may be transforming the job market, but nearly half of U.S. employers believe the technology will make college degrees more valuable over the next five years, according to a new Gallup poll.
The Gallup-Lumina Foundation survey found that 48% of employers expect AI to increase the importance of college degrees, compared with 26% who believe the technology will make them less valuable.
The findings suggest higher education remains a priority for hiring managers despite growing concerns about AI's impact on the workforce.
About 80% of employers said they prefer hiring candidates with college degrees, even for positions that do not require one.
The survey also revealed a divide between employers and the broader public over the value of higher education.
While 60% of employers expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education, just 38% of U.S. adults reported the same in a separate Gallup survey conducted in June.
The findings are based on an August survey of 2,500 U.S. hiring decision-makers.
Pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca is teaming up with tech powerhouse Oracle to use artificial intelligence to identify patients for clinical trials and monitor potential safety risks, in a move aimed at speeding up drug development and improving medical research.
The partnership will combine AstraZeneca's drug development expertise with Oracle's AI technology and healthcare data capabilities to help researchers match patients with clinical trials and identify potential safety concerns.
The collaboration will initially focus on cancer, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, immunology and rare diseases, with the technology potentially helping doctors diagnose serious illnesses earlier.
AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said the partnership could help researchers and healthcare providers improve patient care through AI-driven technology.
"We can help clinicians identify patients sooner, optimize clinical trials, and generate evidence continuously across the lifecycle of a medicine," Soriot said in a statement.
The first project will focus on hypertension research in Abu Dhabi, in partnership with UAE-based healthcare company M42.
Patient recruitment remains a major obstacle in clinical research, with enrollment delays often extending trial timelines and driving up development costs.
AstraZeneca has also faced clinical trial setbacks, including delays involving a breast cancer treatment and the failure of a nerve disorder drug, raising concerns about its drug development efforts, according to Reuters.
The companies have signed a non-binding agreement and have not disclosed financial terms.
The partnership comes as AstraZeneca seeks to expand its drug portfolio and reach more than $80 billion in annual revenue by 2030.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Portuguese police clear housing protest camps, arresting 55
articles.title_zh: Portuguese police clear housing protest camps, arresting 55
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds at Lisbon tent camp demand action, as Giorgia Meloni says march in Italy was exploited by ‘hooligans’
The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal , with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.
A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said that while “the reasons for the protests were understandable, the violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable”.
In Lisbon, a tent camp reminiscent of the one established in Madrid three weeks ago was set up by protesters demanding action to tackle the housing crisis and living costs.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – located in the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital – after a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.
The attenders vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant. “So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating.”
Antonio Margado, a 52-year-old engineer, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data. The impact is especially harsh on younger people and those in Lisbon – around a quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants live in the capital’s greater metropolitan area.
Saturday’s camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents had already been set up.
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs.
Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has said his government understood that people wanted to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”. But he has warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests in France .
after newsletter promotion
There have also been violent demonstrations in Albania this week , where demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of the country’s prime minister, Edi Rama.
On Saturday, protesters threw rocks, molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.
In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began. The protests continued into the night, with buildings – including a court, banks and post office – set on fire or severely damaged.
The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of the US president, Donald Trump.
Growing anger over soaring rents and social inequality boiled over in Spain last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she was unable to pay the 230% rent increase sought by the investment firm that had bought her flat.
The plight of the late María del Carmen Abascal – and the wider issue it embodied – led to street demonstrations and the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital , and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.
In France, fury over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris has snowballed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Jay says UK-based online platform Atom Learning, which offers services to help children prepare for exams, has been down today. Many schools are on half-term this week, which Jay says is a "key time for the current Year 6 kids studying for their 11+ exams to use the platform".

But it says users in this region may "experience elevated errors and intermittent network issues".

"We would like to apologise for any inconvenience and continue to monitor the situation, which is also affecting other organisations."

This is not the first time weâve seen a cloud outage cause a ripple effect across online services.
A year ago, a failure in Amazon Web Servicesâ US infrastructure disrupted apps including Snapchat, Roblox and Duolingo, with consequences around the world.
AWS, Microsoftâs Azure and Google Cloud dominate this market - accounting for almost two-thirds of global spending on cloud infrastructure, according to Synergy Research Group.
So many services that look entirely separate to us actually depend on the same underlying suppliers. A technical problem in one location can reach far beyond it, disrupting businesses and their customers.
It also puts scrutiny on companiesâ back-up arrangements whether they can keep operating when the infrastructure they depend on fails, and how quickly they can switch to working systems elsewhere.
Delivery firm DPD says connection issues affecting its website have now been resolved.
In a statement posted on its Irish X account in the last few minutes, the firm has thanked customers for their patience.
As a reminder, Google said earlier it is "seeing the recovery" of its cloud services.
The latest update from Google says that "we are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritising the recovery of existing workloads".
It also says "tentatively" that the "full recovery of existing workloads should be completed" shortly.
Joe Tidy Cyber correspondent
Itâs not the first time that issues at "Europe-west2" data centres have caused big problems.
In July 2022 there was an outage that was widespread and disruptive at the same cluster of centres.
Google put it down to a cooling failure during a heatwave that forced the company to shutdown a large number of computers to avoid a fire or heat damage.
Data centre computers are powerful and can get very hot if they are not joined up to sophisticated cooling systems like fans or water pipes to extract the heat.
Google said afterwards that it would be conducting a review into cooling systems at its data centres and globally to improve its service.
There is no suggestion that this is the cause of todayâs outage, with the company instead blaming it on a "power event".
But it's another reminder that the digital services we all use are only as resilient as the physical infrastructure they run on.
Liv McMahon Technology reporter
Google Cloud is one of a handful of large cloud computing providers which essentially prop up our digital lives.
Along with bigger players like Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud provides infrastructure and services such as for storage, data management and developer tools, to power and maintain the services we use daily.
Their customers can access these services or tools via specific "regions" - geographical sites which contain a single data centre or a cluster of them.
In this case, the incident causing issues for a number of different companies and platforms - especially Revolut - stems from disruption Google says is affecting "multiple services" at its site Europe-west2, which is based in London.
As Googleâs only UK cloud region, any issues at it can have a large knock-on effect for UK or London-based businesses which might heavily rely on Google Cloud services.
But they can affect companies across Europe or further afield which might use its services - as we saw last October when more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline by an AWS outage at its largest data centre region in the US.
In an updated statement, Google points to a "power event" after problems with its web platform services this morning.
In a statement on its Cloud status platform, it says that they are still suffering "an issue with multiple services".
It adds: "Due to a power event we had suffered an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated.

articles.title_orig: New Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Trailer Is A Throwback To The '90s N64 Ads
articles.title_zh: New Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Trailer Is A Throwback To The '90s N64 Ads
articles.content_orig:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time might not be Nintendo's next Switch 2 exclusive (don't worry Nintendo Switch Sports Resort , we haven't forgotten about you), but the looming 5th November release date means that the marketing campaign is in full swing.
We're getting new trailers, shorts and TV spots all over the place at the moment, and the new 'Art thou ready?' ad shared by Nintendo UK has left us sufficiently hyped and unexpectedly reminded of the N64 original's ads back in the '90s.
The new trailer (above) doesn't feature any fresh footage, but the whole thing is extremely badass. You've got scenes from the game intercut with flaming text screens asking such questions as "Willst thou flee? Or fight?" while bombastic brass tunes blast in the background. Come on, how can that not leave you excited?
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 853k
All of this riffs on the original release's TV trailers, let's not forget. Those employed a similarly OTT backing track (from Conan, no less), and used the same fire text flare, controversially boasting the tagline, "Willst thou get the girl? Or play like one?" — later changed to "Willst thou soar? Or willst thou suck?" for obvious reasons. We've linked one such OG trailer below, so you can see the similarities for yourself.
For a game like Ocarina of Time, it feels only fitting that Nintendo goes hard on the nostalgia for the marketing — who doesn't get a bit misty-eyed thinking about their first time playing it, eh? Only a few weeks to go before we get to dive in all over again!

articles.content_orig:
Converse makes up just 2.5% of Nike’s sales. Last quarter, it accounted for 20% of the company’s sales decline. Two years into Elliott Hill’s tenure as Nike’s CEO, the 118-year-old maker of the Chuck Taylor is a big drag on a comeback that isn’t coming together, with Converse sales down 28% in the most recent quarter and analysts openly wondering whether Nike will keep it in its portfolio.
The brand is enduring an unusually long, deep cold streak. Analysts blame the falloff on Converse’s inability to innovate and its overreliance on the Chuck Taylor model, Fortune’s Phil Wahba reports .
Vans, owned by VF Corp, has had a similarly hard time in recent years for the same reason: over-reliance on skater shoes in distinctive checkered patterns. “We’ve never seen a 44% decline in demand for a brand,” BNP Paribas analyst Laurent Vasilescu noted, citing Converse’s sales deterioration in the fiscal quarter that ended in November 2025. The analyst said he wouldn’t be surprised if Nike ultimately decided to sell off Converse.

Preply analyzed 3,000 Reddit posts and comments about corporate jargon. “Circle back” was the most complained-about phrase, with 203 mentions. It beat “synergy” (181), “bandwidth” (97), “touch base” (96), and “take this offline” (62).
A lot of people don’t seem to know what common business words mean. Among the jargon pulled from Reddit, the most-searched terms were “paradigm,” with 311,000 monthly searches, and “synergy,” with 310,000. After those come “best practice,” with 303,000, and “bandwidth,” with 187,000.

articles.title_orig: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses? : Planet Money
articles.title_zh: What if an AI bubble bursts — and that accelerates AI job losses? : Planet Money
articles.content_orig:
This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here .
What if an AI bubble bursts, triggering a recession, and that recession ends up accelerating the replacement of workers with AI? Call it the AI double whammy.
I've long been skeptical of sweeping claims about how AI will transform the world. I still am. We don't really know. But as this technology advances, I've found myself worrying more about what it could mean for our livelihoods.
Two strands of economic research have given me reason to take this double whammy seriously. One concerns the history of financial bubbles. The other concerns a surprising relationship between recessions and automation, when businesses use technology to do tasks that were previously done by humans.
First, the bubbles. In 1978, the economist Charles Kindleberger published an influential book titled Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises . Drawing on the theoretical work of economist Hyman Minsky, Kindleberger went through centuries of economic history and saw a recurring pattern.
Often the bubble starts with some big potential change to the economy. A revolutionary new technology, for example, that promises to transform industries and create enormous wealth. Investors have a good reason to be excited by it. But they get overly excited. During the upswing, they bet tons of money expecting basically that the sky is the limit. And they often build up debt in the process, borrowing money to make even bigger bets and thereby helping to further fuel the boom. That debt can become a ticking time bomb. When reality sets in, asset prices fall, but those debts remain. Borrowers struggle to repay, lenders suffer losses, and a market crash can spiral into a financial crisis and a painful recession.
One crucial insight is that a technology can truly be revolutionary, yet still fuel a bubble that ends in a financial crash. For example, the railroads. I wrote about that bubble in a previous Planet Money newsletter — and how its collapse triggered "The Panic of 1873." The ensuing economic turmoil helped foment a populist uprising and the first major immigration crackdown in American history.
AI is now basically propping up the U.S. stock market. An analysis from J.P. Morgan earlier this month found that just 42 AI-related companies accounted for around two-thirds of the S&P 500's stock price gains since early 2024. Meanwhile, AI-related companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to help finance data centers and the energy infrastructure to power them.
None of this proves that what we're witnessing is a bubble or that this debt is a ticking time bomb for the financial system. The bursting of the dot-com bubble helped usher in a relatively mild recession. Debt played a smaller role in that boom, helping to limit the financial fallout. Its collapse did not trigger a systemic financial crisis like the one that followed the housing market bust around 2008.
Even without a financial crisis, though, there could be a painful reckoning. Will all these companies ultimately make enough money to justify all their borrowing and spending? Will each company survive? Technology analyst Benedict Evans has warned that fierce competition between companies offering similarly capable AI models could drive down the prices they can charge and leave little room for profit — even as they're spending ungodly amounts of money to develop and run these models.
If an AI bust triggers a recession, that would be painful enough. But this is where a few studies add to my anxieties. Because they suggest that recessions can be the very moment when businesses turn to new technologies to replace workers.
We tend to imagine automation as a gradual process. Technology improves, businesses adopt it, and jobs slowly change or disappear, theoretically while new jobs appear in other parts of the economy. But this research suggests that automation can happen in bursts, and those bursts tend to cluster around recessions.
One study , by economists Nir Jaimovich and Henry Siu, found that jobs vulnerable to previous waves of automation saw most of their decline around recessions. Between 1990 and 2017, 88% of the decline in the share of Americans employed in these jobs occurred during recessions or in the months immediately before or after them.
And here's the unsettling irony: fierce price competition could keep AI companies from delivering the profits investors expect, while making their technology cheaper for other businesses to use to replace workers. If an AI bust triggers a recession, that downturn could accelerate worker replacement. Investors could lose their money, and workers could still lose their jobs.
It's a nightmare scenario. First, the bust hammers our retirement savings. Then, as businesses scramble to cut costs, many of our jobs are permanently lost.
Of course, we still don't know whether AI will deliver enough profits to justify all the borrowing and spending, whether a bust would trigger a painful recession, or whether the automation patterns found in past recessions will repeat themselves with AI. A downturn could leave businesses with less money to invest in AI. And AI could still prove more useful for helping workers get more productive than outright replacing them.
Whether AI delivers one whammy or two whammies or none, there are policies that can limit the damage when workers lose their jobs. Obviously, unemployment insurance and other policies like that. And people like Bill Gates are proposing that we should tax AI and robots , making it more economical to continue employing humans while generating revenue that the government can spend to enhance the safety net. That idea is something we might explore in a future newsletter.
So, yeah, there are reasons this nightmare might never come true, and there are ways to limit the damage if it does. That, however, hasn't stopped me from worrying about it.
But it felt cathartic writing this down — getting these worries out of my head and onto the page.

It will feature Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize-winning professor at MIT who's been critical of AI companies, and Ronnie Chatterji, a professor at Duke and chief economist at OpenAI. articles.title_orig: UK to Fly Missions to Defend Saudi Arabia From Houthi Attacks
articles.title_zh: UK to Fly Missions to Defend Saudi Arabia From Houthi Attacks
articles.content_orig:
The United Kingdom said Tuesday it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen.
The UK will fly “defensive counter-air missions” using Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the defense ministry said in a statement.
Over the past month, the Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, launching ballistic missiles and drones at key infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports.
The UK is already providing air-to-air refueling support to Saudi Arabia and has deployed air defense equipment and British personnel to help protect the kingdom, a Downing Street spokesperson told reporters.
The Typhoons will intercept missiles and drones launched against Saudi Arabia and will not conduct offensive strikes inside Yemen, the spokesperson said.
The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom, following a Saudi attack on the Houthi-controlled airport in the Yemeni capital Sana’a.
They have stepped up their attacks in recent weeks, launching repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. One such strike killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia has looked for military support from regional and western allies to counter the intensified Houthi attacks. France agreed to deploy defense assets, including military personnel and more than 100 American military advisers are on the ground providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly established joint forces command.
Pakistan has forces stationed in Saudi Arabia and the Egyptian parliament is debating whether to send support after President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi called an emergency session to deploy military assistance to the kingdom.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement. “The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region.”
Last month, the Iran-allied rebel group launched a lightning offensive on Yemen’s western coast, capturing key territory, including the Bab al-Mandeb maritime chokepoint on the Red Sea, potentially expanding Tehran’s influence over another trade corridor.
Saudi Arabia cancels next week’s ‘Davos in the Desert’ conference after series of Houthi attacks
Backed by Saudi warplanes, Yemen’s anti-Houthi governmental ground forces have launched a counter-offensive to recapture lost territory.  Despite a heavy airstrike campaign and a large ground offensive, Houthi rebels have remained in control over key locations, and continued launching missiles and drones on their adversaries.
At least 53 newly recruited Yemeni governmental forces were killed in a ballistic missile attack by the Houthis on the southeastern Shabwa province Monday, local officials said.
The attack was condemned by the US mission to Yemen which called it a “cowardly attack by the Iran-backed Houthi militia” on Yemenis who had “volunteered to keep their communities and country safe.”
This story has been updated with additional developments.
James Frater contributed reporting
